newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori sees hostage crisis dragging on.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori sees hostage crisis dragging on.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori said on Thursday he was prepared for the 44-day-old hostage crisis at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima to drag on for several weeks or even months.

"It could go on a lot longer still. I am patient (to wait) for the hostages to be freed safe and sound ... It could take some weeks, some months," Fujimori said in an interview with Argentina's CVN television network.
Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages inside the diplomatic mansion have refused to give up their captives unless the government frees 400 jailed comrades.
Fujimori, who was scheduled to leave later on Thursday for a crisis meeting with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Canada on Saturday, has flatly rejected the rebels' demands.
The meeting in Toronto was aimed at achieving "a very close coordination," he said. "If we were in an emergency situation we would need to be in close contact."
The two leaders also were expected to discuss recent police manoeuvres outside the siege site that have brought sharp criticism from Tokyo.

Police repeatedly blasted broadcasts of martial music, sirens and the roar of aircraft at the building on Thursday in an apparent ploy to wear down the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels' resolve.
The recording of martial music, with aircraft in the background, created the impression helicopters and planes were approaching the fortified compound, witnesses said.
A helicopter and a twin-engine military plane flew over the site and an armoured personnel carrier rumbled close by.
There was no immediate reaction from the rebels, who fired at police on an armoured convoy passing the home on Monday.
Hashimoto has called several times this week for Fujimori to exercise caution in the deployment of police at the site to prevent "accidents or incidents."

But a senior Peruvian government source, speaking on condition of anonymity, insisted Fujimori would not apologise to Hashimoto for the provocative police tactics or seek approval for a military assault on the building.
Fujimori told CVN the police movements were aimed at demonstrating their control of the siege site.
In his first meeting with families of hostages at Government Palace on Thursday, Fujimori assured them he was "trying to find alternatives" to end the crisis.
Fujimori was due to fly from Lima to Toronto in the presidential jet around midnight local time (0500 GMT), accompanied by journalists and officials.

The Peruvian president will then travel to Washington on Sunday for a meeting on Monday with U.S. President Bill Clinton to thank him for Washington's strong backing during the crisis, the government sources said.
Washington did not, however, confirm the meeting.
Hashimoto said on Thursday the weekend summit would confirm Tokyo and Lima's joint strategy of not "caving in to terrorism."
But he is likely to temper tough talk with a plea that Lima avoid provoking the rebels into harming their hostages, who include two dozen Japanese, officials in Tokyo said.
"The meeting is not meddling with the Peruvian government, but is a discussion," government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama said.
Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said his country was chosen to host Saturday's meeting because of its mediating role in the crisis which has been accepted by both sides.

Canada's ambassador to Peru, Anthony Vincent, and Roman Catholic bishop Juan Luis Cipriani -- who have been accepted by both sides to sit on a committee overseeing eventual peace talks -- will also travel with Fujimori.

The MRTA rebels originally seized hundreds of guests when they stormed the residence Dec. 17 during a diplomatic reception. They released most of the captives but kept those they consider the most important bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother, top government and security force officials, two ambassadors, and the Japanese.
